In both cases the instinctive belief is an implicit principle which authorizes the deduction and which cannot have been the work of experience. The principle of the stability of phenomenal connections, and the principle of the necessary precedence of a phenomenon or series of phenomena to every new phenomenon, are two primordial laws of the human intelligence. All reasoning founded on experience implies them. The first is called the empirical principle, because it is that which most directly authorizes experimental deductions: the other is called the principle of causality.

It must not be supposed that these principles present themselves under a general form from the first development of the intelligence. The greater part of men reason with them without their consciousness so much as glimpsing them. They are two instincts by which man is guided without knowing it. They are two movements impressed upon his intelligence by the Author of nature.

III

p. 124

Do los efectos inferimos las causas, como de las causas los efectos, mediante el encadenamiento de fenómenos que llamamos leyes de la naturaleza, Si vemos un movimiento en direccion diferente de la que toman los graves abandonados a sí mismos, inferimos que ha sido producido por un impulso. Si vemos una fruta, no podemos dudar que ha sido desarrollada i formada en una planta por el proceder órdinario de la vejetacion. Si vemos órden, correspondencia de partes, medios dirijidos a la consecución de un fin, deducimos de aquí la existencia de una voluntad que se propuso el fin, de una intelijencia que ideó los medios, i de un poder que los puso en accion. De esta manera fuimos conducidos al conocimiento del adorable Autor de la naturaleza. La armonía maravillosa del universo, donde cada parte parece haber sido hecha para hacer juego con las otras, i todas concurren a la conservacion i propagacion de los entes animados; donde aun el, al parecer, mas [p. 124] pequeño i despreciable de éstos presenta a la vista una trabazon delicada de partes, evidentemente calculadas para obrar juntas, un sistema de necesidados i facultades constantemente correlativas, una simetría de forma que es como la divisa de una intelijencia que ha querido revelarse a otras, una unilormidad de reproduccion que en nada se asemeja a lo que podemos ligurarnos en los efectos de un choque fortuito de átomos; donde cada órgano de cada uno de estos vivientes, cada viscera, cada músculo, cada vaso, cada fibia, es un sistema de máquinas de complicado pero esquisito artificio, lleno a la verdad de misterios para nuestros limitados alcances, pero seguro en sus efectos, expedito en su modo de obrar (que se verifica en la mayor parte de los casos sin la intervencion de la voluntad i aun de la conciencia) i dotado hasta cierto punto de la facultad de resistir a los accidentes i de repararse a sí mismo; donde, por ejemplo, el órgano de la vision, uno de los que mejor conocemos i probablemente uno de los ménos complicados, encierra primores de mecanismo que apenas han podido imitarse eroseramente en los mas acabados iustrumentos de que se gloría la industria humana: esta maravillosa armonía, estas correlaciones, este órden nos obliga a reconocer una causa intelijente, dotada de un poder i sabiduría superiores, fuera de toda comparacion i medida, a los que cl hombre emplea en sus obras,

From effects we infer causes, as from causes effects, by means of the concatenation of phenomena which we call laws of nature. If we see a motion in a direction different from that which heavy bodies take when left to themselves, we infer that it has been produced by an impulse. If we see a fruit, we cannot doubt that it has been developed and formed on a plant by the ordinary process of vegetation. If we see order, correspondence of parts, means directed to the attainment of an end, we deduce from this the existence of a will which proposed the end, of an intelligence which devised the means, and of a power which put them into action. In this manner we were led to the knowledge of the adorable Author of nature. The wonderful harmony of the universe, where each part seems to have been made to play with the others, and all concur in the conservation and propagation of animate beings; where even the, to all appearance, most [p. 124] minute and contemptible of these presents to the sight a delicate framework of parts, evidently calculated to act together, a system of needs and faculties constantly correlative, a symmetry of form which is like the device of an intelligence that has wished to reveal itself to others, a uniformity of reproduction which in nothing resembles what we can figure to ourselves in the effects of a fortuitous collision of atoms; where each organ of each one of these living beings, each viscus, each muscle, each vessel, each fiber, is a system of machines of complicated but exquisite artifice, full indeed of mysteries for our limited reach, but sure in its effects, expeditious in its mode of acting (which takes place in the greater part of cases without the intervention of the will, and even of consciousness) and endowed to a certain point with the faculty of resisting accidents and of repairing itself; where, for example, the organ of vision, one of those which we know best and probably one of the least complicated, contains refinements of mechanism which have scarcely been able to be imitated even grossly in the most finished instruments of which human industry boasts: this wonderful harmony, these correlations, this order oblige us to recognize an intelligent cause, endowed with a power and wisdom superior, beyond all comparison and measure, to those which man employs in his works.

Todas las relaciones de causa i efecto se reducen, como hemos visto, a sucesiones constantes de fenómenos: ¿pero cuál es la causa de esta constancia? ¿Por qué el movimiento sucedo constantemente al impulso, i ciertas sensaciones a ciertas impresiones oreánicas? Reducidos todos los fenómenos del universo alas últimas sucesiones elementales, ¿cuál es el vinculo que une en cada una de ellas los dos hechos contiguos? Este vínculo no puede consistir en un fenómeno o fenómenos intermedios, porque, segun la suposicion, hemos reducido los fenómenos a las últimas sucesiones elementales, i porque en tal caso la nueva serie presentaria nuevos términos sucesivos, cuya relacion constante reproduciria la dificultad en toda su fuerza.

All the relations of cause and effect are reduced, as we have seen, to constant successions of phenomena; but what is the cause of this constancy? Why does motion constantly follow impulse, and certain sensations certain organic impressions? All the phenomena of the universe being reduced to the last elementary successions, what is the bond that unites in each of them the two contiguous facts? This bond cannot consist in an intermediate phenomenon or phenomena, because, according to the supposition, we have reduced the phenomena to the last elementary successions, and because in such a case the new series would present new successive terms, whose constant relation would reproduce the difficulty in all its force.

p. 125

La causa i el efecto son, en último resultado, ciertos hechos que se suceden inmediata i constantemente uno a otro: pero el entendimiento no puede concebir una conexion absolutamente necesaria entre los fenómenos cuya constante sucesion observa. Que el cuerpo A chocando con el cuerpo B le comunique una parte de su fuerza, i le haya mover en cierta direccion i con cierta velocidad, es una cosa que, hablando absolutamente, pudiera no ser. Porque si la conexion entre tales fenómenos fuese de necesidad absoluta, seria preciso suponer en el universo una multitud de causas que destituidas de intelijencia i de voluntad, obrarian sin embargo con el mayor concierto, produciendo de consuno este órden asombroso en que descubrimos a cada paso fines i medios, es decir, voluntad e intelijencia. Por consiguiente, las conexiones que observamos no pueden ser de necesidad absoluta; ellas suponen una causa anterior que las ha querido i coordinado; una causa dotada de voluntad e intelijencia para quererlas i coordinarlas; una causa además cuya conexion con los efectos que ella produce es de necesidad absoluta. Las necesidades comunicadas i secundarias presuponen una necesidad primera, absoluta; i el poder a cuyos actos están ligados los efectos por una necesidad absoluta, no puede existir sino en una voluntad intelijente que quiere los fines i coordina los medios. Ahora bien, ¿qué signilica la sucesion absolutamente necesaria de los efectos a los actos de ese poder en esa voluntad intelijente? ¿qué sienilica la conexion absolutamente necesaria entre sea la luz i la existencia de la luz? Sienilica la omnipotencia, el poder increado, infinito. Poder infinito, porque nada ménos se necesita para sacar de la nada a los séres, i para someter sus fenómenos a conexiones necesarias, con solo quererlo; poder increado, porque si no lo fuese, la conexion entre sus voliciones i los efectos correlativos seria prestada, i nó de necesidad absoluta; poder, por consiguiente, eterno, ino solo soberano, esto es, superior a todos los demas poderes, sino único, porque todos los demas poderes no son otra cosa que emanaciones suyas.

Cause and effect are, in the last result, certain facts which follow one another immediately and constantly: but the understanding cannot conceive an absolutely necessary connection between the phenomena whose constant succession it observes. That the body A, striking against the body B, should communicate to it a part of its force, and make it move in a certain direction and with a certain velocity, is a thing which, speaking absolutely, might not be. For if the connection between such phenomena were of absolute necessity, it would be necessary to suppose in the universe a multitude of causes which, destitute of intelligence and of will, would nevertheless act with the greatest concert, producing jointly this astonishing order in which we discover at every step ends and means, that is, will and intelligence. Consequently, the connections which we observe cannot be of absolute necessity; they suppose an anterior cause which has willed and coordinated them; a cause endowed with will and intelligence to will and coordinate them; a cause moreover whose connection with the effects which it produces is of absolute necessity. Communicated and secondary necessities presuppose a first, absolute necessity; and the power to whose acts the effects are bound by an absolute necessity cannot exist except in an intelligent will which wills the ends and coordinates the means. Now what does the absolutely necessary succession of the effects to the acts of that power in that intelligent will signify? What does the absolutely necessary connection between let there be light and the existence of light signify? It signifies omnipotence, uncreated, infinite power. Infinite power, because nothing less is needed to draw beings out of nothing, and to subject their phenomena to necessary connections, by merely willing it; uncreated power, because, if it were not, the connection between its volitions and the correlative effects would be borrowed, and not of absolute necessity; power, consequently, eternal, and not only sovereign, that is, superior to all other powers, but sole, because all other powers are nothing else than emanations from it.

p. 126

La armonía del universo nos compele, pues, a reconocer un Autor i lejislador todo-poderoso, cuya voluntad ha establecido [p. 126] las conexiones de fenómenos de que resulta el órden jeneral. El poder de las causas inferiores es finito i derivado i el de la primera causa es infinito i propio. Mas, a esto se reduce la diferencia entre las dos especies de causas. La produccion de los efectos de la causa primera es una mera sucesion, como la produccion de los efectos de las otras. Dios quiso que fuese la luz, i la luz fué, es una expresion concreta, pero completa, de la relacion orijinal de causalidad. La idea de uno i otro poder nace de la idea de la constancia i necesidad del efecto, o por mejor decir, es esta misma idea: i si bien es evidente quo la necesidad de los efectos inmediatos de la causa primera, es absoluta, i la de los efectos de las causas secundarias, derivada, no podemos ver en una i otra mas que sucesiones constantes.

The harmony of the universe compels us, then, to recognize an all-powerful Author and Lawgiver, whose will has established [p. 126] the connections of phenomena from which the general order results. The power of inferior causes is finite and derived, and that of the first cause is infinite and proper to itself. But to this is reduced the difference between the two kinds of causes. The production of the effects of the first cause is a mere succession, like the production of the effects of the others. God willed that there should be light, and there was light, is a concrete but complete expression of the original relation of causality. The idea of the one power and of the other arises from the idea of the constancy and necessity of the effect, or rather, is this very idea: and although it is evident that the necessity of the immediate effects of the first cause is absolute, and that of the effects of secondary causes derived, we can see in the one and the other nothing but constant successions.

No estará de mas notar que nos representamos a menudo la deduccion raciocinativa bajo la imájen de la sucesion: «la tierra se mueve en órbitas elípticas; luego hai una fuerza que la hace variar continuamente de direccion.» El segundo juicio decimos que se sigue del primero; que es una consecuencia de él; que pues lo uno es cierto, lo otro no puede ménos de serlo; i ya se sabe que pues (post), aunque aplicado ahora exclusivamente a la posterioridad de razon, significó en su oríjen la posterioridad de tiempo. Todas las lenguas han adoptado esta imájen para representar la deduccion o inferencia, esto es, la operacion intelectual que de un juicio saca necesariamente otro juicio. En los raciocinios demostrativos la conexion entre las premisas i su consecuencia lejítima es de necesidad absoluta.

IV

APÉNDICE 1

It will not be superfluous to remark that we often represent to ourselves rational deduction under the image of succession: “the earth moves in elliptical orbits; therefore there is a force which makes it vary continually in direction.” We say that the second judgment follows from the first; that it is a consequence of it; that since the one is certain, the other cannot but be so; and it is well known that pues [since] (post), although applied now exclusively to posteriority of reason, signified in its origin posteriority of time. All languages have adopted this image to represent deduction or inference, that is, the intellectual operation which from one judgment draws necessarily another judgment. In demonstrative reasonings the connection between the premises and their legitimate consequence is of absolute necessity.

APPENDIX I

p. 127

La idea de la causalidad es una idea de relacion. Con esto solo está dicho que es un producto de la actividad del alma; producto en que el alma saca de las intuiciones i las sensacio[p. 127] nes un concepto que no es resoluble en meras intuiciones i sensaciones.

The idea of causality is an idea of relation. By this alone it is said that it is a product of the activity of the soul; a product in which the soul draws from intuitions and sensations [p. 127] a concept which is not resolvable into mere intuitions and sensations.

Pero la causalidad no es una .relacion elemental sui gene ris; es una relacion compuesta de las de sucesion i de seme-janza.

But causality is not an elementary relation sui generis; it is a relation compounded of those of succession and of resemblance.

Los idcalistas, temerosos de atribuir este concepto relativo a la sensacion, han creido ver en la causalidad algo mas que una sucesion constante. Temor infundado. La sucesion mas simple no puede ser conocida por la sensacion sola, aunque comprendamos bajo este nombre la intuicion pura, absoluta. No puedo, pues, admitir con M. Cousin, que por medio de la sensacion sola (aun incluyendo bajo este titulo los actos de la pura conciencia, llamada metafóricamente sentido íntimo) percibamos la sucesion de un fenómeno a otro. Percibir dos sen=saciones sucesivamente no es lo mismo que percibir la sucesion de las dos sensaciones, o de los dos fenómenos representados por ellas.

The idealists, fearing to attribute this relative concept to sensation, have believed that they saw in causality something more than a constant succession. An unfounded fear. The simplest succession cannot be known by sensation alone, even though we include under this name pure, absolute intuition. I cannot, then, admit with M. Cousin that by means of sensation alone (even including under this title the acts of pure consciousness, metaphorically called inner sense) we perceive the succession of one phenomenon to another. To perceive two sensations successively is not the same as to perceive the succession of the two sensations, or of the two phenomena represented by them.

p. 128

«Si la causalidad,» dice Reid, «no fuese mas que una sucesion constante, se miraria la noche como la causa del dia, i el dia como la causa de la noche.» Para apreciar este argumento en lo que vale, presentémoslo bajo una forma ¡jeneral: el movimiento sucede al reposo; luego, si la causalidad no es mas que una sucesion constante, el reposo es la causa del movimiento. El cuerpo que se calienta pasa siempre de una temperatura inferior a una temperatura superior; luego ésta es efecto de aquella. De la misma suerte, en la luna la menguante será la causa de la creciente, 1 la creciente será la causa de la menguante, etc., ete. Como el sór en que se desarrolla todo nuevo fenómeno deja por precision su estado i toma otro, el estado que se deja deberia siempre mirarse como la causa del estado que se toma. El doctor Reid pudiera haber fortificado su argumento, observando que no es solo constante la conexion de los dos estados, sino necesaria de necesidad absoluta, porque decir fenómeno nuevo es decir transicion de un estado a otro. Ahora bien, ¿no seria absurdo considerar el estado cesante como la causa del estado incipiente? Luego, en la idea de la causalidad, pudiera decir Reid, hai algo mas que la idea do [p. 128] una sucesion constante, i aun algo mas que la idea de una sucesion absolutamente necesaria.

“If causality,” says Reid, “were nothing more than a constant succession, night would be regarded as the cause of day, and day as the cause of night.” To appreciate this argument at its worth, let us present it under a general form: motion succeeds to rest; therefore, if causality is nothing more than a constant succession, rest is the cause of motion. The body which is heated passes always from a lower temperature to a higher; therefore the latter is the effect of the former. In the same way, in the moon the waning will be the cause of the waxing, and the waxing will be the cause of the waning, etc., etc. As the being in which every new phenomenon is developed leaves of necessity its state and takes another, the state which is left should always be regarded as the cause of the state which is taken. Dr. Reid might have strengthened his argument by observing that the connection of the two states is not only constant, but necessary by absolute necessity, because to say new phenomenon is to say transition from one state to another. Now would it not be absurd to consider the ceasing state as the cause of the incipient state? Therefore, in the idea of causality, Reid might say, there is something more than the idea of [p. 128] a constant succession, and even something more than the idea of an absolutely necessary succession.

Este argumento se funda en una torcida intelijencia de lo que se llama fenómeno anterior en la sucesion constante que constituye la causalidad. El que busca la causa de un movimiento, busca un fenómeno que sobreviene al veposo, i es una condicion previa indispensable para que el. cuerpo que está quieto se mueva. El que busca la causa del día, busca un fenómeno que sobreviene a la oscuridad, i es una condicion previa indispensable para que a la oscuridad suceda la luz. El que busca una causa cualquiera, busca un hecho que sobreviene a un estado de cosas, 1 es la condicion previa para la transicion de ese estado a otro. La causa de todo fenómeno incipiente es un fenómeno constante anterior, que sobreviene al estado cesante; que se distingue por consiguiente del estado cesante. Dar el estado cesante por causa del estado incipiente, seria incurrir en una tantolojía ridícula; seria decir, por ejemplo, que si el dia sucede a la noche es porque la noche precede al dia. No es, pues, ni a la noche ni al dia, sino a un fenómeno superviniento, esto es, a la presencia o la ausencia del sol, a lo que conviene, en la teoría de Hobbes i Locke, la nocion de fenómeno antecedente, productivo del dia o la noche.

This argument is founded on a distorted understanding of what is called the antecedent phenomenon in the constant succession which constitutes causality. He who seeks the cause of a motion seeks a phenomenon which supervenes upon the rest, and is an indispensable previous condition for the body which is at rest to move. He who seeks the cause of day seeks a phenomenon which supervenes upon darkness, and is an indispensable previous condition for light to succeed darkness. He who seeks any cause whatever seeks a fact which supervenes upon a state of things, and is the previous condition for the transition from that state to another. The cause of every incipient phenomenon is a constant anterior phenomenon, which supervenes upon the ceasing state; which is therefore distinguished from the ceasing state. To give the ceasing state as cause of the incipient state would be to incur a ridiculous tautology; it would be to say, for example, that if day succeeds night it is because night precedes day. It is not, then, to night or to day, but to a supervening phenomenon, that is, to the presence or the absence of the sun, that the notion of antecedent phenomenon, productive of day or night, belongs in the theory of Hobbes and Locke.

Veamos ahora si son mas fuertes los argumentos con que M. Cousin impuena la fórmula de Hobbes i Locke.

Let us see now whether the arguments with which M. Cousin impugns the formula of Hobbes and Locke are stronger.

«Pregunto, dice M. Cousin, por el hecho solo de suceder un fenómeno a otro, i de sucederle constantemente, ¿será éste la causa de aquel? Cuando decis i pensais que el fuero es la causa de derretirse la cera, ¿entendeis solamente que el derretirse la cera sucede siempre a la aproximacion del fuego? ¿No cretis, no creo todo eljónero humano, que en el fuego hai un no sé qué, una propiedad desconocida que se trata de determinar, i a que se debe referir el fenómeno de la liquidez de la cera?»

“I ask,” says M. Cousin, “whether, by the mere fact that one phenomenon succeeds another, and succeeds it constantly, the former is the cause of the latter? When you say and think that fire is the cause of the melting of wax, do you understand merely that the melting of the wax always succeeds the approach of the fire? Do you not believe, does not the whole human race believe, that in the fire there is a something, I know not what, an unknown property which it is a question of determining, and to which the phenomenon of the liquidity of the wax must be referred?”

p. 129

¿Pero a quése reduce realmente esa ercencia del ¡jénero humano? El no sé qué de la sucesion constante, segun la jeneralidad de los hombres lo concebimos, no es otra cosa que sucesiones constantes intermedias. Si se nos revelan éstas, 1 son de aquellas con que estamos familiarizados, quedaremos pro[p. 129] bablemente satisfechos. Verdad es que 'el filósofo querria ir mas allá. Cuando viese patente a sus ojos el mecanismo del universo, i le fuera posible resolverlo en sus últimas conexiones elementales, aun no estaria contento; querria descubrir el lazo oculto que forma todas esas conexiones. Es de creer, sin embargo, que el filósofo mismo no hace mas en esto, que dejarse llevar del hábito ordinario de inquirir conexiones intermedias en toda conexion percibida. Imajinando que por fuerza ha de llegarse a conexiones elementales, irresolubles en otras, insiste todavía en interpolar en éstas un no sé qué, una cierta actividad en el fenómeno causante, a la cual corresponde una cierta pasividad o susceptibilidad en el fenómeno causado; cualidades ocultas, indefinibles, misteriosas, herencia de la escuela peripatética. Pero la armonía de la naturaleza nos obliga a reconocer que las cualidades que observamos han sido coordinadas por una primera causa intelijente, i que por tanto todas estas potencias, todas estas virtudes particulares, son emanaciones de una virtud o potencia suprema. ¿Estaba ésta sujeta a la necesidad de crear una ajencia intermedia para ligar, en una conexion elemental, el fenómeno A con el fenómeno B, de manera que Á desenvolviese esta ajencia, i por medio de ella obrase en B? ¿I qué seria esto sino colocar entre A i B una conexion intermedia que con igual fundamento tendria que resolverse en otra i otra, hasta el infinito?

But to what does this belief of the human race really reduce itself? The something, I know not what, of the constant succession, as the generality of men conceive it, is nothing else than intermediate constant successions. If these are revealed to us, and are of those with which we are familiar, we shall be probably [p. 129] satisfied. It is true that the philosopher would wish to go farther. When he saw the mechanism of the universe laid open before his eyes, and it were possible for him to resolve it into its last elementary connections, he would still not be content; he would wish to discover the hidden tie which forms all those connections. It is to be believed, nevertheless, that the philosopher himself does nothing more in this than let himself be carried away by the ordinary habit of inquiring after intermediate connections in every connection perceived. Imagining that of necessity we must arrive at elementary connections, irresolvable into others, he still insists on interpolating in these a something, I know not what, a certain activity in the causing phenomenon, to which corresponds a certain passivity or susceptibility in the caused phenomenon; occult, indefinable, mysterious qualities, an inheritance from the peripatetic school. But the harmony of nature obliges us to recognize that the qualities which we observe have been coordinated by a first intelligent cause, and that therefore all these powers, all these particular virtues, are emanations from a supreme virtue or power. Was this subject to the necessity of creating an intermediate agency in order to bind, in an elementary connection, the phenomenon A with the phenomenon B, so that A should develop this agency, and by means of it act upon B? And what would this be but to place between A and B an intermediate connection which, with equal reason, would have to be resolved into another and another, to infinity?

Si no se admite la ajencia primitiva de una causa primera i única, deberia suponerse en cada conexion elemental una necesidad absoluta, i el universo seria entónces el concurso de un número infinito de causalidades independientes, de las cuales no podria resultar el órden armonioso que nuestros sentidos atestiguan.

If the primitive agency of a first and sole cause is not admitted, an absolute necessity would have to be supposed in each elementary connection, and the universe would then be the concourse of an infinite number of independent causalities, from which the harmonious order that our senses attest could not result.

«Supongamos, continua Cousin, que en este momento quisiese yo oir una sonata, i que apenas verificada mi volicion, se hiciese oir esa sonata en el cuarto vecino: en esto es ovidente que no habria mas que sucesion.»

“Let us suppose,” continues Cousin, “that at this moment I wished to hear a sonata, and that, my volition hardly having taken place, that sonata were heard in the neighboring room: in this it is evident that there would be nothing more than succession.”

Yo no he podido nunca hacerme cargo de lo que importa esta hipótesis de M. Cousin. Si en ella se nos exhibe un caso aislado en que la volicion ha precedido casualmente a la sonata, i no FILOSOF,* 9

I have never been able to make out what this hypothesis of M. Cousin amounts to. If it exhibits to us an isolated case in which the volition has casually preceded the sonata, and not

p. 130

uno de infinitos casos en que se haya producido la misma sucesion de fenómenos, ciertamente no habrá en ello mas que una mera sucesion, nó una causalidad, porque la causalidad no es una mera sucesion, sino una sucesion constante, invariable, necesaria, comprobada por su jeneralidad.

one of an infinity of cases in which the same succession of phenomena has been produced, there will certainly be in it nothing more than a mere succession, not a causality, because causality is not a mere succession, but a constant, invariable, necessary succession, verified by its generality.

«Pero yo quiero producir sonidos vocales», dice Cousin, «i los produzco. ¿No pondré aquí entre mis voliciones i los sonidos que pronuncie otra cosa que la sucesion que ántes puse entre mi volicioni la sonata? ¿No es evidente que en el último caso no solo creo que la volicion precede al sonido, sino que creo tambien que la volicion produce el sonido, esto es, que mi voluntad es la causa, i el sonido el efecto?»

“But I wish to produce vocal sounds,” says Cousin, “and I produce them. Shall I here place between my volitions and the sounds I utter anything other than the succession which I before placed between my volition and the sonata? Is it not evident that in the latter case I not only believe that the volition precedes the sound, but believe also that the volition produces the sound, that is, that my will is the cause, and the sound the effect?”

Este es el caso de una verdadera causalidad. ¿Pero qué significan las palabras causa, efecto, produccion en la creencia vulgar, sino sucesion constante, invariable? ¿Que otra cosa es lo que jeneralmente se busca cuando se desea saber una causa?

This is the case of a true causality. But what do the words cause, effect, production signify in the vulgar belief, if not constant, invariable succession? What else is it that is generally sought when one desires to know a cause?

Supongamos, digo yo a mi vez, que álguien hiciese sonar, con solo mandarlo, i como por una especie de majia, un instrumento colocado a cierta distancia, i que las personas presentes oyesen suceder constantemente el sonido al mandato. Como esta sucesion de fenómenos es enteramente nueva para ellas, no mirarian desde luego el mandato como la causa del sonido; pero creerian ligadas las dos causas por medio de sucesiones constantes, intermedias. Luego que se les mostrase el resorte oculto que mueve el que pronuncia el mandato, i el mecanismo que propaga sucesivamente este movimiento hasta las vibraciones del cuerpo sonoro, quedaria satisfecha su curiosidad, i conociendo sucesiones intermedias constantes, que de antemano les eran familiares, creerian haber llegado al conocimiento de la causa, i no desearian saber nada mas. Pararian en esas conexiones intermedias familiares, es decir, en meras sucesiones constantes, comprobadas por su jeneralidad. Tal es el modo en que concibe la relacion de causalidad el comun de los hombres.

Let us suppose, I say in my turn, that someone were to make an instrument placed at a certain distance sound, merely by commanding it, and as it were by a sort of magic, and that the persons present were to hear the sound constantly follow the command. As this succession of phenomena is entirely new to them, they would not at first look upon the command as the cause of the sound; but they would believe the two linked together by means of constant, intermediate successions. As soon as they were shown the hidden spring that moves him who pronounces the command, and the mechanism that propagates this motion successively as far as the vibrations of the sounding body, their curiosity would be satisfied, and, knowing intermediate constant successions which were already familiar to them, they would believe they had arrived at the knowledge of the cause, and would desire to know nothing more. They would stop at those familiar intermediate connections, that is, at mere constant successions, verified by their generality. Such is the way in which the generality of men conceive the relation of causality.

p. 131

El filósofo mismo, cuando desea saber por qué sucede el movimiento de la mano al acto de la voluntad que quiere moverla, no busca ordinariamente otra cosa que conexiones [p. 131] intermedias. Si viese cuál es en el cuerpo animado el órgano que está en comunicacion inmediata con la voluntad; si determinase el primer fenómeno que en ese órgano sucede a la volicion, i toda la serie de fenómenos que se desarrollan sucesivamente en otros órganos, hasta parar en la contracción de ciertos músculos, i si no viese entre cada dos fenómenos sino cenexiones anteriormente conocidas, creeria, i no sin razon, haber hecho descubrimientos importantísimos de causas recónditas que apenas han podido columbrarse de un modo vago i oscuro hasta ahora; i sin embargo, no habria descubierto otra cosa que sucesiones constantes intermedias. Solo la Ontolojía aspira a remontarse. Pero la Ontolojía que se figura en la causalidad elemental otra cosa que una sucesion necesaria, se empeña infructuosamente en dar sustancialidad a una suposicion,

The philosopher himself, when he desires to know why the movement of the hand follows upon the act of the will which wishes to move it, ordinarily seeks nothing else than connections [p. 131] intermediate. If he saw which is, in the animated body, the organ that is in immediate communication with the will; if he determined the first phenomenon that takes place in that organ upon the volition, and the whole series of phenomena that unfold successively in other organs, until they end in the contraction of certain muscles, and if he saw between each two phenomena only connections previously known, he would believe, and not without reason, that he had made most important discoveries of recondite causes which until now have scarcely been glimpsed in a vague and obscure manner; and yet he would have discovered nothing else than intermediate constant successions. Only Ontology aspires to rise higher. But the Ontology which imagines in elemental causality anything other than a necessary succession strives fruitlessly to give substantiality to a supposition.

«Nuestros actos,» dice M. Cousin, «no son solamente fenómenos que aparecen en seguida de las operaciones de la voluntad, sino que los miramos, i los otros hombres los reconocen, como efectos directos de nuestras voliciones. De aquí la imputacion moral, la imputacion jurídica i las tres cuartas partes de la vida i de la conducta humana. Si no hai mas que sucesion entre el acto del homicida i la muerte de su víctima, adios creencia universal de la vida civil toda entera. Toda la vida civil se funda en esta hipótesis jeneralmente admitida: que el hombre es una causa; como la ciencia de la naturaleza se funda en esta otra hipótesis, que los cuerpos son causas, es decir, tienen propiedades que pueden producir tales o cuales efectos. »

“Our acts,” says M. Cousin, “are not merely phenomena that appear in consequence of the operations of the will, but we regard them, and other men recognize them, as direct effects of our volitions. Hence moral imputation, juridical imputation, and three fourths of human life and conduct. If there is nothing but succession between the act of the homicide and the death of his victim, farewell to the universal belief of all civil life. All civil life is founded on this generally admitted hypothesis: that man is a cause; as the science of nature is founded on this other hypothesis, that bodies are causes, that is, have properties which can produce such or such effects.”

p. 132

Esta me parece la parte mas flaca del raciocinio de M. Cousin. Lo que constituye la imputabilidad, la moralidad de los actos humanos, es la volicion en que principian, i lo mismo suponen esa volicion los que han abrazado en esta parte la doctrina de Hobbes, que M, Cousin i su escuela. Que el asesino ponga en accion un no sé qué, o que se desarrolle, solo porque él lo quiere, i en virtud de sucesiones constantes establecidas por el Autor de la naturaleza, una serie de movimientos, de fenómenos, cuyo último término cs la agonía de [p. 132] la víctima, importa lo mismo para la responsabilidad que la naturaleza i las leyes imponen.

En lo que sigue tenemos la satisfaccion de estar enteramente de acuerdo con el ilustre jefe de la escuela ecléctica.

«No solo hai en el entendimiento la idea de causa, no solo creemos que somos la causa de nuestros actos, i que ciertos cuerpos son causas de los movimientos de ciertos otros, sino que tambien juzgamos de un modo jeneral que un fenómeno cualquiera no puede empezar a existir sin una causa que determine esta existencia. En esto hai mas que una idea; hai un principio, i el principio es tan incontestable como la idea. Imajínese un movimiento, una mudanza cualquiera: inmediatamente que concebis esa mudanza, ese movimiento, 0s es imposible no suponer que ha sido producido por una causa. No se trata de saber qué causa sea ésta; lo que importa saber es si el espíritu humano puede concebir una mudanza sin concebir que la ha producido una causa...... No digo yo que no hai efecto sin causa; proposicion frívola, en que un término contiene el otro, i no hace mas que expresar la misma idea de un modo diverso. Como efecto es correlativo a causa, decir que el efecto supone la causa, es decir que el efecto es efecto. Pero no se profiere una proposicion idéntica i frivola cuando se dice que todo fenómeno que principia tiene necesariamente una causa. Los dos términos de esta proposicion no se contienen recíprocamente; el uno es distinto del otro; i con todo, el espiritu ve entre ellos un vínculo necesario. Esto es lo que se llama el principio de causalidad.»

Hemos sentado que el principio de causalidad es instintivo; i que léjos de sernos dado por la experiencia, todos los conocimientos experimentales lo suponen (a); pero admitida la pro-

This seems to me the weakest part of M. Cousin’s reasoning. What constitutes the imputability, the morality, of human acts is the volition in which they begin, and those who have embraced in this matter the doctrine of Hobbes suppose this volition no less than M. Cousin and his school. Whether the assassin puts in action an I know not what, or whether there unfolds, only because he wills it, and by virtue of constant successions established by the Author of nature, a series of movements, of phenomena, whose last term is the agony of [p. 132] the victim, is the same for the responsibility which nature and the laws impose.

In what follows we have the satisfaction of being entirely in agreement with the illustrious chief of the eclectic school.

“Not only is there in the understanding the idea of cause, not only do we believe that we are the cause of our acts, and that certain bodies are causes of the movements of certain others, but we also judge in a general manner that any phenomenon whatever cannot begin to exist without a cause that determines this existence. In this there is more than an idea; there is a principle, and the principle is as incontestable as the idea. Imagine a movement, any change whatever: the instant you conceive that change, that movement, it is impossible for you not to suppose that it has been produced by a cause. The question is not what this cause may be; what matters is to know whether the human mind can conceive a change without conceiving that a cause has produced it. . . . I do not say that there is no effect without a cause; a frivolous proposition, in which one term contains the other, and which does no more than express the same idea in a different manner. As effect is correlative to cause, to say that the effect supposes the cause is to say that the effect is effect. But an identical and frivolous proposition is not uttered when it is said that every phenomenon that begins has necessarily a cause. The two terms of this proposition do not contain each other reciprocally; the one is distinct from the other; and yet the mind sees between them a necessary bond. This is what is called the principle of causality.”

We have laid it down that the principle of causality is instinctive; and that, far from being given to us by experience, all experimental knowledge supposes it(a); but, admitting the instinctive propensity

(a) Some philosophers have pretended to demonstrate the principle of causality

p. 133

(a) Algunos filósofos han pretendido demostrar el principio de causalidad de este modo. Si un nuevo fenómeno existiese sin causa, seria su causa la nada, lo produciria la nada; lo cual es absurdo, porque si la nada produjese algo, tendria ya una accion real, una cualidad positiva, seria por consiguiente algo. Segun ellos, el teorema de la causalidad se deriva de este otro: La nada no produce nada. Lo que [p. 133] pension instintiva de la razon humana a suponer a todo nuevo fenómeno una causa, nada se sigue de ella a favor de éste o aquel modo particular de concebir las causas.

El principio de causalidad, anda siempre unido con aquel otro principio instintivo en virtud del cual, observada en circunstancias dadas una conexion de fenómenos en cierto número de casos, la extendemos a todos los casos en que se ha presentado o en que en iguales circunstancias seguirá presentándose el primero de esos fenómenos. Este principio de la perpetuidad de las leyes a que vemos sujetas las conexiones fenomenales, es la base de todos los conocimientos que adquirimos por la experiencia i lo hemos llamado por eso principio empírico. (a)

«Tan cierto es,» dico M. Cousin, «que no es do los sentidos i del mundo exterior de donde nos viene el principio de causalidad, que sin la intervencion de este principio, el mundo exterior, de donde quiere Locke sacarlo, no existiria para nosotros. En efecto, suponiendo que un fenómeno pudiese principiar en el tiempo o en el espacio sin que fuéseis irresistiblemente impelidos a atribuirlo a una causa; cuando a los ojos de la conciencia aparece el fenómeno de la sensacion, no buscar- Íais una causa para este fenómeno, no desearíais saber a qué hai de cierto es que los hombres, desde una época mui temprana de la razon, han admitido la causalidad, nó como una verdad derivada, sino como un verdadero principio, que los guiaba en sus raciocinios por una especie de instinto.

in this manner. If a new phenomenon existed without a cause, its cause would be nothing, nothing would produce it; which is absurd, because if nothing produced something, it would already have a real action, a positive quality, and would consequently be something. According to them, the theorem of causality is derived from this other: Nothing produces nothing. What [p. 133] of human reason to suppose a cause for every new phenomenon, nothing follows from it in favor of this or that particular way of conceiving causes.

The principle of causality always goes united with that other instinctive principle by virtue of which, a connection of phenomena having been observed in given circumstances in a certain number of cases, we extend it to all the cases in which the first of those phenomena has presented itself, or in which, in like circumstances, it will continue to present itself. This principle of the perpetuity of the laws to which we see the phenomenal connections subject is the basis of all the knowledge we acquire by experience, and for that reason we have called it the empirical principle.(a)

“So certain is it,” says M. Cousin, “that the principle of causality does not come to us from the senses and the external world, that without the intervention of this principle the external world, from which Locke would derive it, would not exist for us. In effect, supposing that a phenomenon could begin in time or in space without your being irresistibly impelled to attribute it to a cause; when the phenomenon of sensation appears before the eyes of consciousness, you would not seek a cause for this phenomenon, you would not desire to know to what

is certain is that men, from a very early epoch of reason, have admitted causality, not as a derived truth, but as a true principle, which guided them in their reasonings by a sort of instinct.

(a) Might not the principle of causality be resolved into the empirical principle?

p. 134

(a) ¿No pudiera resolverse el principio de causalidad on el principio empirico? En otros términos, ¿no somos conducidos a suponer a todo nuevo fenómeno otro fenómeno que lo acarrea, porque en la esfera de nuestras observaciones ciertos nuevos fenómenos son a menudo acarreados por ciertos otros fenómenos, i porque una analojía instintiva nos hace extender este acarreo a todos los nuevos fenómenos inobservados e inobservables? Creo que concebimos el principio de causalidad como necesario. No podemos concebir que brote en el tiempo un nuevo fenómeno sin que alguna causa lo produzca. El principio de causalidad no se deriva, pues, lójicamente de otro alguno i nace espontáneamente en el entendimiento porque asi lo ha querido el Autor de la naturaleza. [p. 134] se refiere; 0s pararíais en el fenómeno mismo; no alcanzaríais jamás al mundo exterior. ¿Qué es menester para que alcanceis al mundo exterior i conjetureis su existencia? Es menester que, dada una sensacion, os veáis forzados a preguntaros cuál es la causa de este nuevo fenómeno; i que en la doble imposibilidad de referir este fenómeno a vosotros mismos, i de no referirlo a una causa, os veáis en la precision de referirlo a una causa distinta de vosotros, a una causa extraña, a una causa exterior. La idea de una causa exterior de nuestras sensaciones, tal es la idea fundamental de lo externo, de los objetos exteriores, de los cuerpos, del mundo. Elimínese el principio de causalidad, la sensacion queda sola a la vista do la conciencia, i no nos revela otra cosa que su conexion con el yo que la experimenta (a), sin revelarnos lo que la produce, el no yo, los objetos exteriores, el mundo. Se dice muchas veces, i los filósofos lo dicen con el vulgo, que los sentidos nos descubren el mundo exterior; no sin razon, si se quiere decir que sin los sentidos, sin la sensacion, sin este fenómeno antecedente, el principio de causalidad careceria de base para alcanzar a las causas exteriores, i jamás concebiríamos el mundo; pero se engañarian completamente los que creyesen que los sentidos mismos, directamente, sin la intervencion de la razon, (b) sin la intervencion de otro principio distinto, nos dan a conocer el mundo exterior. La razon sola conoce; conoce el mundo exterior, i no lo conoce desde luego sino a titulo de causa. El principio de causalidad es por consiguiente, no temo decirlo, el padre del mundo exterior; tan léjos está de ser cierto que lo saquemos del mundo exterior; i que se derivo de la sensacion. Cuando se habla de los objetos exteriores i

(a) Ni aun esto debemos conceder a la sensacion. Concebir la sensacion en el yo, es concebir una relacion de identidad; es enjendrar a consecuencia de la sensacion, algo que no es sensacion.

In other terms, are we not led to suppose for every new phenomenon another phenomenon that brings it about, because in the sphere of our observations certain new phenomena are often brought about by certain other phenomena, and because an instinctive analogy makes us extend this bringing about to all new phenomena unobserved and unobservable? I believe that we conceive the principle of causality as necessary. We cannot conceive that a new phenomenon should spring up in time without some cause producing it. The principle of causality is not, therefore, logically derived from any other, and arises spontaneously in the understanding because the Author of nature has so willed it. [p. 134] it refers; you would stop at the phenomenon itself; you would never reach the external world. What is needed that you may reach the external world and conjecture its existence? It is needed that, a sensation being given, you should find yourselves compelled to ask what is the cause of this new phenomenon; and that, in the twofold impossibility of referring this phenomenon to yourselves and of not referring it to a cause, you should find yourselves under the necessity of referring it to a cause distinct from yourselves, to a foreign cause, to an external cause. The idea of an external cause of our sensations, such is the fundamental idea of the external, of external objects, of bodies, of the world. Eliminate the principle of causality, and sensation remains alone in view of consciousness, and reveals to us nothing else than its connection with the I that experiences it(a), without revealing to us what produces it, the not-I, external objects, the world. It is often said, and philosophers say it with the vulgar, that the senses discover to us the external world; not without reason, if it is meant that without the senses, without sensation, without this antecedent phenomenon, the principle of causality would lack a basis from which to reach external causes, and we should never conceive the world; but those would be completely deceived who should believe that the senses themselves, directly, without the intervention of reason,(b) without the intervention of another distinct principle, make known to us the external world. Reason alone knows; it knows the external world, and does not know it at first except as a cause. The principle of causality is therefore, I do not fear to say it, the father of the external world; so far is it from being true that we derive it from the external world, and that it is derived from sensation. When one speaks of external objects and

(a) Not even this are we bound to concede to sensation. To conceive the sensa‐

tion in the I is to conceive a relation of identity; it is to engender, in consequence of the sensation, something that is not sensation.

(b) The psychological formula of reason, “it is the faculty of conceiving relations,”

p. 135

(b) La fórmula psicolójica de la razon «es la facultad de concebir relaciones», facultad intuitiva, sise quiere, pero cuyos actos no deben confundirse ni con la sensacion, ni con la mera intuicion, en que el alma se limita a contemplar una afección suya, sin concebirla como suya, sin concebir relacion alguna. [p. 135] del mundo sin admitir previamente el principio de causalidad, no se sabe lo que se dice, i se incurre en un paralojismo. »

an intuitive faculty, if you will, but whose acts must not be confounded either with sensation, or with mere intuition, in which the soul confines itself to contemplating an affection of its own, without conceiving it as its own, without conceiving any relation. [p. 135] of the world without previously admitting the principle of causality, one does not know what one says, and falls into a paralogism.”

Nuestros lectores percibirán la armonía de esta doctrina con nuestra exposicion de los fenómenos de la percepcion sensitiva. Hemos visto que la referencia objetiva deducida de la experiencia, i sobre todo de la experiencia táctil, supone una referencia fundamental a que el mismo tacto no alcanza, la referencia de las percepciones táctiles a una causa distinta del yo. Esa referencia fundamental nos es dada por el principio de causalidad.

Our readers will perceive the harmony of this doctrine with our exposition of the phenomena of sensitive perception. We have seen that the objective reference deduced from experience, and above all from tactile experience, supposes a fundamental reference to which touch itself does not attain, the reference of tactile perceptions to a cause distinct from the I. This fundamental reference is given to us by the principle of causality.

Fácil es ver que admitido este principio como universal ¡ necesario, nada nos obliga a concebir la causalidad como la concibe Mr. Cousin.

It is easy to see that, this principle being admitted as universal and necessary, nothing obliges us to conceive causality as M. Cousin conceives it.

«El resultado de todo esto», dice el ilustre caudillo de la cscuela ecléctica, «es que, si se trata de la idea de causa, no podemos hallarla en la sucesion de los fenómenos sensibles; que la sucesion es la condicion del concepto de causa, nó su principio i su razon lójica; i que si no se trata solamente de la idea de causa, sino del principio de causalidad, resiste todavía mas a la tentativa de explicarlo por la sucesion i la sensacion. En el primer caso se confunde el antecedente de una idea con la misma idea; en el segundo se hace venir de los fenómenos del mundo exterior aquello precisamente sin lo cual no habria para nosotros exterioridad ni mundo; se confunde no ya el antecedente con el consiguiente, sino el consiguiente con el antecedente, la consecuencia con su principio; porque el principio de causalidad es el fundamento necesario hasta del conocimiento mas lijero del mundo, hasta de la mas débil sospecha de su existencia; i explicar el principio de causalidad por el espectáculo del mundo, que solo ha podido sernos dado por ese principio, es explicar el principio por la consecuencia.»

“The result of all this,” says the illustrious leader of the eclectic school, “is that, if it is a question of the idea of cause, we cannot find it in the succession of sensible phenomena; that succession is the condition of the concept of cause, not its principle and logical reason; and that if it is a question not merely of the idea of cause but of the principle of causality, it resists still more the attempt to explain it by succession and sensation. In the first case the antecedent of an idea is confounded with the idea itself; in the second there is made to come from the phenomena of the external world that very thing without which there would be for us neither exteriority nor world; what is confounded is no longer the antecedent with the consequent, but the consequent with the antecedent, the consequence with its principle; because the principle of causality is the necessary foundation even of the slightest knowledge of the world, even of the faintest suspicion of its existence; and to explain the principle of causality by the spectacle of the world, which could only have been given to us by that principle, is to explain the principle by the consequence.”

p. 136

El concepto de sucesion, es necesario repetirlo, no nos es dado por la sensacion, ni por la mera intuicion: es un juicio; es obra de aquella facultad especial a que atribuimos los juicios 1 los raciocinios; es obra de la razon. Purificado así su oríjen, las nociones de que él forma parte, pertenecen, como él mismo, al dominio de una facultad mas elevada que la sensa= [p. 136] cion i que la mera intuicion. Las sensaciones i las meras intuiciones provocan los conceptos de sucesion, los ocasionan, anteceden necesariamente a ellos i en este sentido los producen, nó como elementos de ellos, sino como previas condiciones. Pero enjendrado el concepto de sucesion, entra, nó como condicion previa, sino como elemento constitutivo en la idea de causa.

The concept of succession, it is necessary to repeat, is not given to us by sensation, nor by mere intuition: it is a judgment; it is the work of that special faculty to which we attribute judgments and reasonings; it is the work of reason. Its origin being thus purified, the notions of which it forms a part belong, like itself, to the domain of a faculty higher than sensation [p. 136] and than mere intuition. Sensations and mere intuitions provoke the concepts of succession, occasion them, necessarily precede them, and in this sense produce them, not as elements of them, but as previous conditions. But the concept of succession once engendered, it enters, not as a previous condition, but as a constitutive element, into the idea of cause.

El error de Locke no consiste, a mi parecer, en confundir la idea de causa con la idea de sucesion constante, sino en confundir con las sensaciones las ideas de relacion, productos de la actividad intelectual, conceptos de la razon pura: ¡en esto no ha errado ménos la escuela ecléctica que la escuela de Locke,

Locke’s error consists not, in my opinion, in confounding the idea of cause with the idea of constant succession, but in confounding with sensations the ideas of relation, products of the intellectual activity, concepts of pure reason: and in this the eclectic school has erred no less than the school of Locke.

p. 137

Cuando hablamos de concepto de sucesion, de semejanza, de causalidad, i suponemos su existencia en una época temprana de la razon, no debemos figurarnos que estas ideas se presenten al entendimiento infantil como al entendimiento adulto, o mas bien, como al entendimiento filosófico. Todos los axiomas, todos los principios que dirijen la razon humana, han sido en su oríjen meros instintos, tendencias raciocinativas que obraban de un modo práctico, i que mucho mas tarde (en la gran mayoría del jénero humano, nunca) se presentan al espíritu como fórmulas jenerales. Mucho ántes que el entendimiento jlegase a decirse en abstracto, sí dos o mas cosas son iguales a una tercera, son iguales entre sí, ya habia dicho muchísimas veces, que dos cosas concretas eran iguales entre sí, porque eran iguales a una tercera cosa, tambien concreta. Observando, por ejemplo, que en los dos platillos de la balanza, A se equilibraba con Bi B con C, dedujimos instintivamente que B se equilibraba tambien con C, sin necesidad de que la conciencia contemplase aquel principio bajo su forma jeneral i abstracta. Pero, es forzoso reservar este asunto para cuando tratemos de la jeneralizacion, del juicio i del raciocinio. Contentémonos con reconocer desde ahora dos principios, dos tendencias raciocinativas: el principio de causalidad, que nos hace suponer a todo nuevo fenómeno una causa, i el principio empírico, que nos hace suponer la constancia de las le[p. 137] yes a que están sujetas las conexiones fenomenales que observamos.

When we speak of the concept of succession, of resemblance, of causality, and suppose their existence at an early epoch of reason, we must not imagine that these ideas present themselves to the infant understanding as to the adult understanding, or rather, as to the philosophic understanding. All the axioms, all the principles that direct human reason have been in their origin mere instincts, reasoning tendencies that worked in a practical manner, and that much later (in the great majority of the human race, never) present themselves to the mind as general formulas. Long before the understanding came to say to itself in the abstract, if two or more things are equal to a third, they are equal to each other, it had already said very many times that two concrete things were equal to each other because they were equal to a third thing, also concrete. Observing, for example, that in the two scales of the balance, A was in equilibrium with B, and B with C, we deduced instinctively that B was in equilibrium also with C, without the need of consciousness contemplating that principle under its general and abstract form. But it is necessary to reserve this subject for when we treat of generalization, of judgment and of reasoning. Let us content ourselves with recognizing from now two principles, two reasoning tendencies: the principle of causality, which makes us suppose a cause for every new phenomenon, and the empirical principle, which makes us suppose the constancy of the laws [p. 137] to which the phenomenal connections we observe are subject.

En lo que hemos dicho hasta aquí, hemos prescindido de la intervencion de la voluntad humana en las conexiones fenomenales. Pero, ántes de pasar adelante, i para completar la nocion de la causalidad, es indispensable tomar en cuenta la existencia de una especie particular de causas.

In what we have said hitherto, we have left out of account the intervention of the human will in the phenomenal connections. But before going further, and to complete the notion of causality, it is indispensable to take into account the existence of a particular kind of causes.

Todo fenómeno físico se puede considerar a un mismo tiempo, como efecto ¡como causa, Como efecto está ligado necesariamente al conjunto de antecedentes que lo determinan; i como causa tiene la misma conexion necesaria con el fenómeno o fenómenos que segun las leyes de la naturaleza física está destinada a producir.

Every physical phenomenon may be considered at one and the same time as effect and as cause. As effect it is necessarily linked to the aggregate of antecedents that determine it; and as cause it has the same necessary connection with the phenomenon or phenomena which, according to the laws of physical nature, it is destined to produce.

Un acto de la voluntad, una volicion, es un fenómeno como cualquiera otro, si se considera como causa. Yo quiero mover un brazo, i lo muevo; entre estas dos cosas la conexion es tan necesaria como entre la chispa que cae sobre un monton de pólvora i la explosion de la pólvora. Pero considerada una volicion como efecto, entre ella i su antecedencia no parece haber el mismo enlace necesario que entre dos fenómenos puramente físicos. Creo que nuestra conciencia nos atestigua que la volicion es libre: que en el mismo acto de querer una cosa sujerida por los antecedentes, podemos suspender el imperio de la voluntad a nuestro arbitrio e introducir un fenómeno nuevo, una volicion diferente, que no parece estar ligada con los antecedentes de un modo necesario.

An act of the will, a volition, is a phenomenon like any other, if it is considered as cause. I wish to move an arm, and I move it; between these two things the connection is as necessary as between the spark that falls upon a heap of powder and the explosion of the powder. But a volition considered as effect does not seem to have, between it and its antecedent, the same necessary tie that exists between two purely physical phenomena. I believe that our consciousness attests to us that volition is free: that in the very act of willing a thing suggested by the antecedents, we can suspend the empire of the will at our pleasure and introduce a new phenomenon, a different volition, which does not seem to be linked with the antecedents in a necessary manner.

Hai, pues, dos especies de causas. Las unas son ciegas i 08clavas, por decirlo así, porque obedecen a una antecedencia que determina de todo punto la accion que ejercen, sin que le sea dado rehusarla ni modificarla. Así un cuerpo Á que está en movimiento i choca con el cuerpo B, no puede obrar en B sino precisamente del modo particular determinado por su propia masa, por la direccion que lleva, por la velocidad con que se mueve i por otras ajencias dinámicas.

There are, then, two kinds of causes. The one kind are blind and slavish, so to speak, because they obey an antecedent that determines in every point the action they exert, without its being given them to refuse or modify it. Thus a body A that is in motion and strikes the body B can act upon B only in the precise particular manner determined by its own mass, by the direction it takes, by the velocity with which it moves, and by other dynamical agencies.

p. 138

Otras causas hai, dotadas de intelijencia i voluntad, que, o desarrollan espontáneamente su accion, o, si una antecedencia las provoca, no se someten ciega i servilmente a ella, sino [p. 138] que, o rehusan la accion solicitada, o la modifican a su arbitrio. ¿No pudiera yo, por ejemplo, ejecutar un movimiento en virtud de una determinacion espontánea i caprichosa de mi voluntad? i dado que un antecedente o concurso de antecedentes me indujese a moverme, ¿no pudiera yo modificar a mi arbitrio esta accion, rehusarla, o entre varias maneras de ejecutarla, conducentes al fin que en ella me propongo, elejir arbitrariamente una?

Yo sé mui bien que muchos reclamarán contra esta division, i rechazarán la segunda especie de causas como inconcebible, mirando el elemento de espontaneidad o eleccion con que las caracteriza, como un efecto sin causa, en manifiesta oposicion al principio de causalidad. Pero, si por razones irrefragables nos vemos obligados a reconocer que existen causas dotadas de espontancidad i de eleccion, en una palabra, causas libres, i que sin ellas no puede concebirse el universo, ¿no será preciso inferir que el principio de causalidad no es tan universal como muchos creen, o debe entenderse en un sentido diverso del que mas comunmente se le da?

There are other causes, endowed with intelligence and will, which either develop their action spontaneously, or, if an antecedent provokes them, do not submit blindly and servilely to it, but [p. 138] either refuse the action solicited, or modify it at their pleasure. Could I not, for example, execute a movement by virtue of a spontaneous and capricious determination of my will? and, supposing that an antecedent or concurrence of antecedents induced me to move, could I not modify this action at my pleasure, refuse it, or, among various ways of executing it, conducive to the end I propose to myself in it, choose one arbitrarily?

I know very well that many will protest against this division, and will reject the second kind of causes as inconceivable, regarding the element of spontaneity or election with which they are characterized as an effect without a cause, in manifest opposition to the principle of causality. But if, for irrefragable reasons, we find ourselves obliged to recognize that there exist causes endowed with spontaneity and election, in a word, free causes, and that without them the universe cannot be conceived, must we not infer that the principle of causality is not so universal as many believe, or must be understood in a sense different from that in which it is most commonly taken?

Mr. J. Stuart Mill(a) has peremptorily denied the existence of these causes. “Correctly conceived,” he says, “the doctrine called Philosophical Necessity is simply this: that, given the motives which are present to an individual’s mind, and given likewise the character and disposition of the individual, the manner in which he will act may be unerringly inferred; that if we knew the person thoroughly, and knew all the inducements which are acting upon him, we could foretell his conduct with as much certainty as we can predict any physical event. This proposition I take to be a mere interpretation of universal experience, a statement in words of what every one is internally convinced of. No one who believed that he knew thoroughly the circumstances of any case, and the characters of the different persons concerned, would hesitate to foretell how all of them

p. 139

Mr. J. Stuart Mill (a) ha negado perentoriamente la existencia de estas causas. «Concebida,» dice, «correctamente la doctrina dela llamada necesidad filosófica, se reduce simplemente a esto: que, dados ciertos motivos en el alma, i dado asimismo el carácter i disposicion del individuo, puede colejirse de esta antecedencia, sin miedo de error, la conducta que ese individuo observará; i que si le conociésemos perfectamente, i supiésemos todos los antecedentes que le solicitan, podríamos anunciar su conducta con tanta certidumbre como podemos predecir un hecho físico cualquiera. Para mí esta proposicion es meramente la interpretacion de la experiencia universal; la expresion de una cosa de que todos están íntimamente convencidos. Nadie que creyese conocer las circunstancias de un caso cualquiera i los caracteres de las diferentes personas que en él interviniesen, vacilaria en pronosticar lo que cada una de ellas la) Sistem of Logic, libro VI, cap. 2. [p. 139] haria. Si le ocurriese duda, seria por no saber con toda certidumbre si le eran exactamente conocidas las circunstancias del caso o los caracteres de las personas, nó por imajinarse que teniendo ese conocimiento pudiera caber incertidumbre alguna en su juicio. Ni se crea que esta plena seguridad pugne en lo mas minimo con lo que se llama sentimiento íntimo de nuestra propia voluntad. No nos sentimos ménos libres porque aquellos de quienes somos intimamente conocidos estén tambien seguros de nuestro proceder futuro en circunstancias dadas. Al contrario, miraríamos como una señal de que ignoraban nuestro carácter, o de queno le hacian justicia. Los metafísicos relijiosos que proclaman el libre albedrío, sostienen al mismo tiempo que es compatible con la presciencia divina; i si lo es con ésta, ¿por qué no lo será con otra? Yo puedo ser libre, isin embargo podrá haber algun otro que tenga razon para estar completamente cierto del uso que haré de mi libertad en un caso dado. La doctrina, pues, que considera nuestras voliciones i acciones como consecuencias indefectibles de los estados anteriores del alma, no contradice a nuestra conciencia ni contiene nada derogatorio de la dignidad humana. »

(a) System of Logic, Book VI, chap. 2. [p. 139] would act. Whatever degree of doubt he may in fact feel, arises from the uncertainty whether he really knows the circumstances, or the character of some one or other of the persons, with the degree of accuracy required; but by no means from thinking that if he did know these things, there could be any uncertainty what the conduct would be. Nor does this full assurance conflict in the smallest degree with what is called our feeling of freedom. We do not feel ourselves the less free, because those to whom we are intimately known are well assured how we shall will to act in a particular case. We often, on the contrary, regard the doubt what our conduct will be, as a mark of ignorance of our character, and sometimes even resent it as an imputation. The religious metaphysicians who proclaim free-will maintain at the same time that it is compatible with the divine foreknowledge; and if it is with this, why not with another? We may be free, and yet another may have reason to be perfectly certain what use we shall make of our freedom. It is not, therefore, the doctrine that our volitions and actions are invariable consequents of our antecedent states of mind, that is either contradicted by our consciousness, or felt to be degrading.”

p. 140

Esta argumentacion de Mr. Mill rueda toda sobre una hipótesis inverificable. ¿Qué hombre sensato puede linsojearse de haber penetrado hasta en los mas recónditos pliegues del corazon ajeno, o aun del suyo propio? En los motivos mismos, ¿qué multitud de pequeños accidentes no podrá haber que se nos escondan, o nos parezcan insignificantes, no siéndolo? I una hipótesis inverificable, ¿cómo podrá ser materia de una experiencia universal? La j¡jeneral conviecion que Mr. Mill invoca a su favor no se extiende a mas que reconocer la influencia de motivos poderosos que si en la mayor parte de los casos dominan al corazon, en ninguno lo arrastran con irresistible violencia. Ni veo cómo pueda conciliarse con el sentimiento íntimo de mi propia libertad la persuasion de que otro sea capaz de predecir con una seguridad completa cuál ha de ser mi conducta en circunstancias dadas. Ni cabe argilir de la presciencia divina a la humana. El Sér Eterno está presente a todos los instantes de la duracion de sus obras: para la Diyi[p. 140] nidad no hai pasado ni futuro, como los hai para las intelijencias creadas.

This argumentation of Mr. Mill turns wholly upon an unverifiable hypothesis. What sensible man can flatter himself that he has penetrated into the most recondite folds of another’s heart, or even of his own? In the motives themselves, what a multitude of little accidents may there not be that are hidden from us, or seem to us insignificant, though they are not so? And an unverifiable hypothesis, how can it be the matter of a universal experience? The general conviction which Mr. Mill invokes in his favor extends no farther than to recognizing the influence of powerful motives which, if in the greater part of cases they dominate the heart, in none sweep it along with irresistible violence. Nor do I see how the persuasion that another is capable of predicting with complete assurance what my conduct is to be in given circumstances can be reconciled with the inner feeling of my own liberty. Nor is it permissible to argue from the divine foreknowledge to the human. The Eternal Being is present to all the instants of the duration of His works: for the Divinity [p. 140] there is neither past nor future, as there are for created intelligences.

«Pocos hai,» continúa Mr. Mill, «a quienes la mera constancia de la sucesion parezca dar un vínculo bastante estrecho a una relacion tan peculiar como la de causa i efecto. Aunque la razon repudia, la imajinacion retiene el concepto de una conexion mas íntima, de un lazo « special, de una conexion efectiva ejercitada por el antecedente sobre el consiguiente; i esto es lo que, aplicado a la voluntad humana, pugna con nuestra conciencia i subleva nuestros sentimientos. Estamos seguros de que sobre nuestras voliciones no hai esa enerjía coercitiva. Los que piensan que las causas acarrean sus efectos por un lazo mistico, tienen razon de creer que la relacion entre nuestras voliciones i sus antecedentes es de otra naturaleza. »

“There are few,” continues Mr. Mill, “to whom mere constancy of succession appears a sufficiently stringent bond of union for so peculiar a relation as that of cause and effect. Even if the reason repudiates, imagination retains, the feeling of some more intimate connexion, of some peculiar tie, or mysterious constraint exercised by the antecedent over the consequent. Now this it is which, considered as applying to the human will, conflicts with our consciousness, and revolts our feelings. We are certain that, in the case of our volitions, there is not this mysterious constraint. Those who think that causes draw their effects after them by a mystical tie, are right in believing that the relation between volitions and their antecedents is of another nature.”

En otra parte he manifestado mi opinion sobre ese no sé qué misterioso; pero no por eso hai razon de afirmar que no pudiera existir sin que nuestra conciencia lo percibiese. ¿Qué importa explicar la causalidad por la mera constancia de la sucesion, si al mismo tiempo se pretende que la universalidad de eso principio se extiende a los fenómenos de la voluntad humana de la misma manera que a los de la pura materia?

In another place I have expressed my opinion about that mysterious I know not what; but that is no reason for affirming that it could not exist without our consciousness perceiving it. What does it matter to explain causality by the mere constancy of succession, if at the same time it is claimed that the universality of that principle extends to the phenomena of the human will in the same manner as to those of pure matter?

Segun Mr. Mill, la conviccion de que podemos modificar nuestras inclinaciones si queremos, es todo el sentimiento interno de la libertad moral de que tenemos conciencia. Un individuo se siente moralmente libre, si siente que las tentaciones no lo dominan, sino él a ellas; i si, aun cediendo a ellas, sabe que puede resistirles, i que si tratase de sacudir su yugo, no habria menester para esto un deseo mas imperioso que el que le es dado desarrollar, si quiere. Pero en éste si quiere significa una volicion como otra cualquiera. ¿Puede ella desarrollarse en el alma sin una antecedencia que necesariamente la produzca, i de todo punto la determine? Somos libres. ¿Es ello la consecuencia indefectible de cierto concurso de antecedentes? La libertad humana no existe.

According to Mr. Mill, the conviction that we can modify our inclinations if we will is the whole inner feeling of moral liberty of which we are conscious. An individual feels himself morally free if he feels that the temptations do not dominate him, but he them; and if, even when yielding to them, he knows that he can resist them, and that if he tried to shake off their yoke he would need for this no more imperious desire than that which it is given him to develop, if he will. But in this if he will there is meant a volition like any other. Can it develop itself in the soul without an antecedent that necessarily produces it, and in every point determines it? We are free. Is that the unfailing consequence of a certain concurrence of antecedents? Human liberty does not exist.

p. 141

Supongamos que la libertad humana no exista, i que nuestras voliciones no sean mas que fenómenos acarreados constantemente por otros fenómenos: resta averiguar si no aparece en [p. 141] el universo ningun otro elemento de espontaneidad i eleccion, A lo ménos es cierto que el gran sistema de causalidades que el universo nos presenta principia en una causa primera; i no puede ménos que suponerse en ella una volicion que en la produccion del universo ha sido espontánea i libre. Esta volicion ha sido, por consiguiente, un hecho sin una causa que de todo punto lo determinase; una excepcion al principio de causalidad. 1 admitida esta excepcion, es evidente que el prin-cipio de causalidad, en el sentido que jeneralmente se toma, no es necesario de necesidad absoluta; i que si está sujeto a una excepcion, puede estarlo igualmente a otras. En suma, no es un principio universal.

Let us suppose that human liberty does not exist, and that our volitions are nothing more than phenomena constantly brought about by other phenomena: it remains to inquire whether there does not appear in [p. 141] the universe any other element of spontaneity and election. It is at least certain that the great system of causalities which the universe presents to us begins in a first cause; and it cannot be otherwise than supposed that in it there was a volition which in the production of the universe was spontaneous and free. This volition was, consequently, a fact without a cause that in every point determined it; an exception to the principle of causality. And this exception admitted, it is evident that the principle of causality, in the sense in which it is generally taken, is not necessary with an absolute necessity; and that if it is subject to one exception, it may be equally so to others. In short, it is not a universal principle.

Se dirá talvez que el principio de causalidad se refiere únicamente a los hechos nuevos, porque, no pudiendo concebirse que éstos salgan por sí mismos de la nada, es preciso asignarles una antecedencia que los determine. Pero, una volicion que produjo la creacion fué necesariamente un hecho nuevo en la escala infinita del tiempo; i si respecto del Sér Eterno nada es viejo ni nuevo, porque para el Sér Eterno no hai ántes ni después, para la razon humana los hai, i a esta misma cadena de existencias sucesivas en que se versa la razon humana, es a la que damos la creacion por principio. Por otra parte, si el principio de causalidad fuese necesario de necesidad absoluta, la eternidad misma estaria sujeta a su imperio.

It will perhaps be said that the principle of causality refers solely to new facts, because, as these cannot be conceived to come out of nothing by themselves, it is necessary to assign them an antecedent that determines them.
